news.hook: Samuel Tunick handed border agents a special code that erased his smartphone's data in seconds. Now, the Atlanta activist faces up to five years in prison for what prosecutors call deliberate evidence destruction.
news.name: Activist Faces Felony for Wiping Phone at Border with Duress Code
news.summary: On January 24, 2025, Tunick returned from the Dominican Republic to Atlanta's airport, where Customs agents demanded his Google Pixel phone's passcode during secondary inspection, initially citing child exploitation concerns but later linked to terrorism suspicions from his activism. Instead of his real passcode, he gave 'Killmenow,' a GrapheneOS duress feature that instantly wiped all data and encryption keys. Charged under a rare federal statute for destroying property to prevent seizure, his defense argues the warrantless search violated his rights and that using a built-in privacy tool isn't obstruction; a judge has yet to rule after a July 2026 hearing. The case divides opinions and has travelers turning to burner phones, testing border authority over encrypted devices.
